cards.title: Two Ground Rules Before Investing in Ecommerce Analytics
cards.summary: Data analytics only pays off when metrics are measured before you need them and every report ends in a decision, not a dashboard.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether your store is ready to spend on analytics tools or headcount, or auditing why your current reporting isn't changing any store decisions.
steps: Accept the first truth: if you can't measure it, you can't improve it. If you never calculate cost of acquisition before running paid ads, you can't tell whether a campaign lowered or raised it. Same for email: without channel-level revenue tracking you can't know if this send beat the last one.

Accept the second truth: collecting and organizing data is only half the job; the output must inform a decision. A report nobody acts on is 'mindless self-indulgence' in the source's words, not analytics.

Start collecting data points now even if they aren't valuable yet (order history, haircut-style CRM records in the source's example). Early datasets compound in value when the business and budget are larger.
Prioritize analysis around the unknown variables in the business — the questions where you can't currently say which lever to pull — rather than re-reporting metrics you already understand.

Size your investment to the business: the source's heuristic is that a $1M business might make $5K–$15K decisions from good analytics while a $100M business might make $1M–$10M decisions, so analytics spend should scale with revenue, counting both tools and the human time to interpret them.
caveats: The dollar ranges are the source's illustrative heuristics, not benchmarks derived from a formula.
Analytics investment assumes someone can turn reports into digestible, decision-ready output; without that, spend is wasted.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: Qualitative vs Quantitative Ecommerce Data: What and Why
cards.summary: Quantitative data tells you what changed on your store; qualitative data tells you why customers acted, and both are needed.
cards.use_when: Interpreting a conversion-rate change on a PDP or landing page and deciding what to fix next.
steps: Treat quantitative data as the what and how: e.g., you changed the page copy and conversion rate moved. This is what most analytics tools and dashboards provide.
Recognize its limits: quantitative results leave the driver unexplained. Was the new headline better because customers related to it, or because it activated fear?

Collect qualitative data to answer the why — through customer conversations, surveys, quizzes, long-form feedback. The source calls it messier and often more expensive to obtain (research partners, interviews), which is why teams default to dashboards.
Pair them: use quantitative signals to find which page, channel or product moved, then use qualitative input to explain the driver and generate the next test hypothesis.
Expect the two to conflict and decide deliberately which to trust for that decision rather than defaulting to whichever is easier to pull.
caveats: Qualitative collection often requires budget or staff time (interviews, panels, research vendors).
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: Zero, First and Third-Party Data for Ecommerce Attribution
cards.summary: Zero-party data is what customers tell you, first-party is what you track, third-party is external enrichment — and they frequently disagree.
cards.use_when: Reconciling attribution across ad platforms, post-purchase surveys and CRM data, or planning what customer attributes to enrich for segmentation.
steps: Classify your sources: zero-party = customer explicitly tells you (post-purchase survey, quiz, feedback form); first-party = you track it directly on your site (purchase history, on-site behavior); third-party = aggregated external sources (Experian, large platforms).

Expect conflict at the attribution layer: an analytics platform may credit a Google ad click while the post-purchase survey says 'a friend told me.' Someone must decide how to attribute and record that rule.

Use zero-party long-form answers as raw copy material — build a word board from what customers say they liked or the pain the product solved, then adjust headlines or product descriptions to match their language.
Use third-party enrichment for triggers: e.g., if you sell furniture, flag which customers just became homeowners and time outreach around that event.
Route quiz and survey data into your CRM/ESP rather than leaving it in a standalone tool — siloed quiz data can't drive segmentation or personalization.
caveats: Keep privacy/compliance considerations in view; the source notes data is bought and sold through back-office exchanges and declines to give legal guidance.
Third-party availability and accuracy vary by region and provider — verify current data coverage before building triggers on it.

cards.title: Collect Customer Feedback at Every Lifecycle Stage
cards.summary: Ask customers questions before purchase, after purchase and after churn — not just at checkout — because founders who stop talking to customers weekly lose the why.
cards.use_when: Designing a voice-of-customer program to feed PDP copy, merchandising, retention and win-back campaigns.
steps: Map the stages where you ask: before they've heard of you (market research), as a prospective visitor on-site, after purchase, and after churn — for physical products set a timeline like 'hasn't bought in a year' and interview those people.

Use open-ended on-site questions at the point of hesitation: the source cites Hotjar-style prompts such as 'what is this page missing?' because long-form answers surface concrete blockers ('couldn't find the price,' 'couldn't find my color,' 'I still don't understand what you do').

Run a simple one-question post-purchase survey ('where did you buy this?' / 'where did you hear about us?') to sharpen attribution, typically more useful for larger stores fine-tuning their attribution model.
Have founders or senior operators talk directly to customers; the source's rule of thumb is at least one customer conversation per week in the first three years of a business.
For quizzes, pick tools that push data points into your CRM and return personalized recommendations immediately — the recommendation is where the quiz earns its keep, not the data collection alone.
caveats: Tool examples (Hotjar, Fairing, Octane AI, Typeform) reflect the source's era — verify current features and integrations before committing.
Decide in advance which feedback to act on; not every comment should change the store.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: The 3% Rule for Qualitative Feedback
cards.summary: Focus qualitative listening on your 3% most loyal and 3% most dissatisfied customers rather than the 94% in the middle.
cards.use_when: Choosing which customers to interview or survey when you have limited research time and need the highest-signal input for product, offer or retention decisions.
steps: Segment your customer base to isolate the extreme ends: top ~3% most loyal and bottom ~3% biggest detractors (the source attributes this framing to a ProfitWell founder).
Interview the loyal group to learn exactly what you do well — the language, benefits and moments that make them repeat buyers — and reuse that language in PDP copy, ads and email.
Interview the detractors to learn what not to do and where the experience broke; treat these as fix-list inputs for fulfillment, support or product pages.
Treat the middle 94% as lower priority for deep qualitative work — they respond to aggregate quantitative tracking instead.
Feed findings into concrete changes: headline and description rewrites from loyal-customer language, operational fixes from detractor complaints.
caveats: 3% is the source's heuristic, not a calculated threshold; adjust to your list size so each group has enough respondents.
Extreme customers may not represent the median buyer — use their input for why and what-not-to-do, and quantitative data for how-widespread each issue is.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: Don't Let the HiPPO Pick Your Ecommerce Metrics
cards.summary: Using data to defend a pre-existing opinion (Highest Paid Person's Opinion) suppresses profitable tests — build the test and let results, not titles, decide.
cards.use_when: When a founder, CMO or director overrides a proposed test on brand or 'that's how we've always done it' grounds — e.g., homepage merchandising, product imagery or promotion placement.
steps: Separate the two modes: using data to support your decision vs. letting data reveal its own position. Watch for selective citation of supporting graphs and quiet shelving of contradicting ones.

On product imagery, the source's observation is that white-background shots are generally not the highest converting — lifestyle or action shots often perform better — but the correct move is to test on your own site rather than swap everything on one person's say-so.

If a stakeholder insists everything must match strict brand guidelines, ask what the missed opportunity costs: the source cites a beauty-box homepage where removing four subscription-length options to a single add-to-cart was projected to add roughly $1M/month in revenue, and the test result was vetoed for retention-metric reasons.
Reframe objections as 'can we do both?' — keep the annual option available on the second page while simplifying the entry point, so brand and retention goals aren't necessarily sacrificed.
When you must act on opinion because no data exists (e.g., launching a new live event), treat the launch itself as the data-collection event and design the next iteration from what you learn.
caveats: The $1M/month figure is one company's test result, not a promise or benchmark.
The source's author admits he does not make all of his own decisions from data; the principle is to reduce the handicap of opinion-led choices, not to eliminate judgment.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: Pick One Primary Metric: Customers, Revenue or Profit
cards.summary: A company can typically optimize for only one of three top-level metrics at a time — customers, revenue or profit — and each sub-metric should ladder to it.
cards.use_when: Setting the quarter's focus for acquisition, pricing or cost decisions, or resolving arguments between departments optimizing different numbers.
steps: Choose exactly one primary metric from the three: number of customers, revenue, or profit. You can occasionally get lucky and move two, but the source says you almost never optimize all three simultaneously.

Understand the trade: maximizing customer count pushes price down or free (the source's hyperbolic example is infinite customers at zero price, and bankruptcy); revenue sits in the middle with a reasonably priced product that must still make money per sale; profit generally implies the highest pricing.
Map each department's sub-metrics to that primary metric rather than letting them optimize locally (e.g., conversion rate, AOV, referral coefficient, retention).
Note the interdependencies: raising conversion rate can lower customer quality and lifetime value; raising AOV can also reduce LTV. Decide which trade-offs you accept.

Fix the primary metric for a long horizon — roughly annual — because swapping it weekly or monthly creates organizational turmoil. The source suggests big focus swings (now loyalty, now acquisition) should be quarterly, bi-annual or annual initiatives.
caveats: The three-metric framework is the source's model; revenue and profit can move together for periods, so don't overstate the exclusivity.
Short 'quick win' KPI pushes (reviews, referral coefficient, loyalty points used, purchase frequency) are fine as sidelights without changing the company focus.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: Match KPI Focus to Your Company Stage
cards.summary: Early-stage stores optimize for customer count and can lose money doing it; mature or steady stores can shift to profit and cost reduction.
cards.use_when: Deciding ad spend, discount depth and growth targets for a store that has found product-market fit versus one that is happy with its market.
steps: Early stage: prioritize customers, because more customers drive virality, referrals and brand breakout; the source notes this is why early-stage companies often lose money — they buy customers and rely on future LTV.

Growth stage: the source's preferred profile for tooling advice is brands doing roughly $1M–$10M/year who have found product-market fit and are adding staff — they face inventory, cash flow, service inquiries and analytics needs that tools solve well.
Pivoting stage: there is often a moment to shift from customers to revenue, and later to profit.

Steady million-dollar business example: the source suggests a store content with its market might optimize for profit — accept $900K instead of $1M but keep $100K by cutting opex, reducing headcount or going after only the cheaper-to-acquire customers via lower ad spend.
Larger bankrolls justify longer time horizons; a small startup may need the next customer tomorrow, but still must avoid burning that customer with a sub-optimal experience.
caveats: The $1M–$10M range is the source's preferred client profile for a tooling advisor, not a rule about who should invest in analytics.
Choosing profit over growth is framed as a legitimate lifestyle-business choice, not a failure.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: Compounders vs Linear Metrics in Ecommerce
cards.summary: Conversion rate and referral coefficient compound revenue and customer growth, so prioritize them over one-off linear levers.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest next month's budget in CRO, referral program, or a linear traffic/spend increase.
steps: When analyzing any metric, classify it: is this comp1ounding, incremental or one-off? The source flags conversion rate and referral coefficient as compounding.

Illustrate the compounding logic: if conversion rate rises and you would have made $10,000 this month, the same traffic next month makes roughly $10,100 before any other change, because the improved rate applies on top of everything else.
Referral logic: with 100 customers this month and referral coefficient moving from 5% to 10%, next month you get 110 customers instead of 105 from the same input.

Implication for sequencing: start with conversion rate optimization because it is one of the highest levers and early stores want it; only when you feel you're at the top of that S curve (every extra dollar into CRO returns less) should you shift focus to AOV, cross-sell/upsell, partnerships, post-purchase affiliate offers, or LTV initiatives.

Use comparative metrics, not single-line graphs: revenue vs. AOV, revenue vs. profitability, revenue vs. new customers, revenue broken out by channel — a revenue-up-month-over-month chart alone doesn't explain how or which lever to pull.
caveats: The arithmetic examples are illustrative of compounding logic, not measured outcomes.
The source's position that CRO should come first is his opinion; it assumes you have enough traffic to measure conversion changes reliably.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: Watch What Your Winning Metric Breaks
cards.summary: Optimizing one metric can quietly damage lifetime value, customer quality or brand, so track the metrics your decision touches.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a conversion tactic with brand or quality side effects — misspelled-ad testing, aggressive discounting, or AOV-boosting bundles.
steps: Before scaling a winning test, list the secondary metrics it could move: conversion rate up can mean lower-quality customers and lower LTV; AOV up can also reduce LTV depending on how it's forced.

Consider the source's agency example: an agency raised ad conversion by intentionally misspelling ads, which worked for clicks/conversions but damaged brand affinity. The source argues a brand team could reasonably reject that conversion gain as not worth the long-term brand cost.
Apply the same lens to store merchandising: forcing a larger subscription commitment or higher-priced bundle on the entry page may lift AOV but hurt the customer relationship and eventual LTV.

When you know the trade-off, estimate whether customer experience reduction is offset by the metric gain before shipping; the source prefers alignments where on-site experience and conversion improve together.
Escalate trade-off decisions to whoever owns the primary metric (see the customers/revenue/profit choice), since local teams will otherwise optimize their own number.
caveats: Brand damage from tactics like misspellings is argued as a long-term, hard-to-measure cost — the source presents it as a consideration, not a measured result.
Some LTV effects (higher AOV reducing LTV) are described as possible rather than universal.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: When to Change KPIs: The Top-of-S-Curve Test
cards.summary: Change your core focus when additional spend on your best lever returns less and less — not on a weekly or monthly whim.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether to keep pushing CRO, shift budget to LTV/retention work, or reallocate to acquisition channels.
steps: Track return on each lever over time; when every additional dollar into conversion-rate optimization yields diminishing returns, you're at the top of that S curve and it's a signal to change focus.

At that point, move to the next lever: AOV via merchandising, cross-sell and upsell, co-marketing partners, post-purchase affiliate offers, or selling to existing, past and churned customers (LTV work, which the source says tends to align more closely with profit maximizing than customer or revenue maximizing).
Set the cadence: large focus shifts belong on quarterly, bi-annual or annual cycles. Weekly or monthly swings between 'now we do loyalty, now we scale acquisition' create turmoil.

Keep small quick-win pushes separate from the big focus: a few weeks targeting review count, referral coefficient, loyalty points used, products per order, or purchase frequency is fine without resetting the department's north star.
Use comparative charts to make the call — a single metric going up or down doesn't show which lever is saturating.
caveats: The S-curve threshold is a judgment call, not a numeric cut-off; the source gives no specific ROI floor.
Diminishing returns on CRO don't mean stop CRO entirely — they mean stop making it the primary focus.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: Predictive Analytics and AI Execution in Ecommerce
cards.summary: Analytics has moved from humans explaining charts to AI recommending actions — and increasingly executing them — so stores that adopt predictive tools and AI-run tests are positioned to outcompete slower adopters.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to apply AI in merchandising, ad creative, attribution, on-site conversion or customer service, or fending off 'AI will hurt our brand' objections.
steps: Understand the shift: previously all analysis meant organizing data, choosing comparative metrics, and having a human explain the graph; now predictive tools use past data and regression-style machine learning to estimate, e.g., that a 5% ad-spend increase will move new customers and revenue while cost of acquisition stays roughly steady.

The next step the source predicts is AI not just predicting but executing: generating and running landing-page or creative variants, reading conversion rate as the objective, and feeding results back to improve the next generation.

Set human boundaries rather than hands-on involvement: guardrails like 'no misspelled words, no profanity' while letting the system test broadly — adding humans slows the loop and makes it less data-driven.

Expected near-term displacements named by the source: media agencies need fewer people for running tools (strategy remains), creative and content-writing teams shrink toward one editor, customer service largely automates with escalation, and merchandising can be AI-selected, including testing demand before placing a purchase order.
Adapt rather than resist: the source notes brands blocked by antiquated practices or a HiPPO veto on AI in customer service risk cost structures that competitors beat.
caveats: These are the source's predictions for the next three to five years, not observed results — treat timelines as speculative.
The 'one in a thousand' customer-service problem rate is the speaker's estimate, not a benchmark; test escalation paths before fully automating.
cards.source_name: eCommerce Marketing Data 101_ Derric Haynie's Crash Course on Understanding Data Analytics.docx

cards.title: Start Collecting Store Data Before It's Worth Anything
cards.summary: The value of an early data set is optionality: you can't analyze history you never recorded, so log data points now that only pay off at larger scale.
cards.use_when: Setting up tracking, CRM fields or operational records for a store that hasn't started paid acquisition or advanced analytics yet.
steps: Inventory what you currently capture and what future questions you might want to answer — the source's salon example: haircut styles, visit frequency (every two months), day of week (Saturdays), even photos, which together can predict the business.
Record data points even when the use case isn't clear yet; early data sets are more valuable later when budget and revenue are larger.
Don't wait for paid ads to calculate cost of acquisition — you can and should compute it before running paid advertising.
Commit to organizing and keeping data, since most businesses can't answer questions retrospectively if they never logged the fields.
Pair collection with an owner who can turn reports into digestible, decision-ready output; analytics spend includes both tools and the human analysis cost.
caveats: Collecting everything indefinitely creates cost and clutter — the source frames it as collecting data points that might interest you, not exhaustive logging.
The salon example is an illustration of the principle, not a proven ecommerce playbook.
